newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee called to open 1.00-2.00 cents higher.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee called to open 1.00-2.00 cents higher.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures were called to open 1.00 to 2.00 cents per lb higher on Monday, although some traders said the market was likely to come in closer to unchanged.
"It's called higher on paper," said one trader. "And London did not make its due, but I think we'll open near unchanged."

London robusta futures were called as much as $30 lower, but fell well short of its due and traded tightly mixed at midday on Monday. At break, benchmark LIFFE September was off $3, to $1,780, after sinking to a low of $1,776.

Friday, New York arabica futures ended mixed in thin trading, with September rising 3.20 cents, to 169.30, after ranging from 173.00 to 166.25. Spot July finished 0.35 cent weaker, at 189.90, while the outer months closed up 2.90 to down 2.85.
The July/September switch shrank to 20.60 cents, from 24.15 cents at the close on Thursday, while September/December widened to 20.30 cents compared with 19.85 cents.
Technically, traders pegged September resistance at the 174.00-175.00 level, with the next upside hurdle at 181.00 cents. Strong support was seen at 165.00 cents.
After Friday's close, CSCE reported certified coffee stocks fell by 280 60-kg bags as of June 26, to 45,893 bags. There were 14,594 bags pending grading, the exchange said.
Also after the close on Friday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture released its bulletin Tropical Products: World Markets & Trade.

USDA estimated 1997/98 world coffee exports at 84.4 million 60-kilogram bags, up from a revised 82.9 million bags seen in 1996/97. USDA previously pegged 1996/97 world coffee exports at 79.6 million bags.
USDA said total coffee supply in producing countries in 1997/98 is forecast at 130.5 million bags, down 2.5 percent from the prior year largely due to the lower beginning stock levels.

The USDA data showed 1997/98 beginning stocks of coffee in producing countries at 26 million 60-kg bags, their lowest level since 1980/81. It forecast 1997/98 ending stocks in producing countries at 20 million bags.
Earlier this month, USDA forecast 1997/98 world coffee production at 103.7 million bags and estimated the Brazil crop at 28.0 million bags.
On the weather front, no damaging cold is expected this week in Brazil's coffee belt, U.S.-based forecaster Weather Services Corp said on Monday.
